problem: Multi-robot research shares task assignments, maps and training data, but not the internal state produced by each robot's agentic loop (memory, plan progress, skill experience), which stays private inside each robot. A newly arrived robot therefore starts from scratch.
motivation: Embodied AI is becoming agentic (memory, execution-time planning, self-evolution), and real deployments increasingly involve several robots in the same changing space. If one robot has explored a room or found a blocked corridor, others should not have to rediscover it, so the team needs shared, validated records of world state, task progress and skills.
key_idea: Embodied Collective Intelligence (ECI): a shared layer in which a robot team pools world memory (Co-Perception), a task-state ledger (Co-Action) and a skill library (Co-Evolution), so that a new robot inherits team state while sensing and acting remain local.
insight: The case study suggests that the benefit of shared memory comes from the merged memory covering more objects and regions than any single robot's memory, not just from having more entries. A newcomer with the merged memory of A and B reaches 77.1% SR and 82.5% SR (text and image queries), against 24.1% SR for a newcomer with no memory and about 54-58% for robots with half the memory. With memory, SPL nearly tracks SR, while from-scratch search wanders (SPL 0.172 vs SR 0.241). Only the world-memory component is tested, so Co-Action and Co-Evolution remain untested.
method: Co-Perception: distributed observations are written into a shared world memory, with timestamps, observer labels, freshness indicators and event history, and only compact updates are synchronized.
Co-Action: a shared task-state ledger of claims, progress, failures, released commitments and help requests; a logical (non-central) scheduler exposes conflicts and triggers reassignment.

Co-Evolution: local attempts enter a skill pool, are categorized, deduplicated and merged into a skill library; each record stores task type, preconditions, embodiment requirements, evidence count and verification status.
Inheritance test: a newly arrived robot reads world memory, the task ledger and compatible skills before acting, and still verifies locally.

Case-study agent: retrieves entries from an open-vocabulary semantic memory index built from past RGB-D trajectories; Qwen3.5-Plus chooses between navigating to a remembered location and free exploration (Uni-NaVid as the VLN model), and loops until the target is reached.

setting.backbone: Qwen3.5-Plus (VLM agent reasoner, frozen) + Uni-NaVid (VLN model for exploration)
setting.training_data: none (training-free composition of pretrained models; memory built from prior robot trajectories)
setting.observation: egocentric RGB-D with poses, detected objects and semantic cues, plus retrieved memory
setting.action_space: high-level choice between navigating to a remembered location and free exploration; Uni-NaVid low-level VLN actions
setting.privileged: none stated; robots A/B/D use memory from prior trajectories through the scene (pre-exploration memory)

results: A newcomer robot inheriting merged team memory reaches 77.1% SR / 0.757 SPL (text query) and 82.5% SR / 0.809 SPL (image query). This compares with 24.1% SR / 0.172 SPL for a no-memory newcomer and about 54-58% SR for robots holding half the memory. It is an illustrative study, not a benchmark-level evaluation.
limitations: A conceptual/position paper: only the shared world-memory component is tested, on 4 HM3D scenes and 166 tasks; Co-Action and Co-Evolution are unevaluated.
No comparison against existing multi-robot or memory-based navigation baselines; there are no ablations of memory freshness, staleness or communication cost.
Open issues acknowledged: stale information, cross-embodiment transfer, communication overhead, safety and responsibility boundaries.
